You've seen this picture. Ape, to stooped ape-man, to upright human, marching left to right.
It's been copied, printed and parodied for sixty years.
There's just one problem. It's wrong.
The idea is older than the picture.
In 1874, the German biologist Ernst Haeckel drew the human story as a tree.
Simple life at the roots. Fish and apes up the trunk.
And at the very top, alone: Man.
Human evolution wasn't a ladder. It was a bush.
Charles Darwin had already seen it. In 1837, in a private notebook, he sketched this.
Above it, he wrote two words. I think.
Branches splitting, and splitting again. Most of them ending.
No top. No finish line. Just whatever is still growing.
So let's draw our bush. Start about seven million years ago, in what is now Chad.
This skull, nicknamed Toumaï, may sit close to where our line split from chimpanzees'.
Some researchers say it walked upright. Others aren't convinced.
Three point six million years ago, in Tanzania, someone walked through wet volcanic ash.
Those footprints, at Laetoli, survive. Upright, two-footed walking.
Around the same time lived Lucy, found in Ethiopia in 1974.
About three point two million years old. A small brain, but legs built for walking.
The ladder makes her a rung on our way up. The truth is messier.
Jump to Kenya, about one and a half million years ago.
On one muddy lakeshore, two different human relatives left their footprints.
One was Homo erectus. The other was Paranthropus boisei, with huge jaws for tough food.
Two branches, side by side. Neither is thought to be the other's ancestor.
Homo erectus travelled further than any human relative before it.
Its fossils turn up from Africa to Georgia, China and Java.
And it lasted. On Java, the last known Homo erectus lived around a hundred and ten thousand years ago.
That's more than one and a half million years for one species.
In Morocco, fossils about three hundred thousand years old show an early form of our own species.
Some experts call them early Homo sapiens. Others, a step on the way.
Around the same time, in a South African cave, lived Homo naledi.
Its brain was less than half the size of ours.
Yet it lived just a few hundred thousand years ago, not millions.
In Europe and western Asia, there were the Neanderthals.
Their brains were as large as ours.
Across Asia lived the Denisovans, known mostly from DNA, first read from a finger bone in 2010.
On the island of Flores lived Homo floresiensis, about a metre tall.
And in the Philippines, Homo luzonensis, named in 2019.
Put the dates side by side, and the ladder falls apart.
A little over a hundred thousand years ago, as many as six kinds of human may have been alive at once.
If your ancestors lived outside Africa, around two percent of your DNA likely comes from Neanderthals.
Some people in Papua New Guinea carry several percent Denisovan DNA.
Our ancestors didn't only replace these people. They met them, and had children with them.
Then, one by one, the other branches ended.
Neanderthals vanish from the record around forty thousand years ago.
The youngest Homo floresiensis bones are around sixty thousand years old.
Today, only one kind of human is left. Us.
So why does the ladder still feel right?
The palaeontologist Stephen Jay Gould argued that the picture shows what we expect to see.
A ladder has a top. And we get to stand on it.
Even brains didn't climb in a straight line. Homo floresiensis had a brain about the size of a chimpanzee's, and still made stone tools.
A bush has no top. Just survivors, and all the branches that didn't make it.
We're not the top of a ladder. We're the last twig left on a bush that was once crowded with other ways of being human.
